entities.summary:
Onomacritus (fl. late sixth–early fifth century BCE) was an Athenian chresmologue—collector and editor of oracles—associated with the Peisistratid court and with early work on Homeric texts. Ancient anecdotes cast him as both learned compiler and forger: Herodotus reports his exile for interpolating oracles, a story that reveals how prophetic books were political instruments in archaic Athens. This pivotal figure stands at the intersection of tyranny, cult, and textual innovation, reflecting the complex dynamics of ancient Athens during its most turbulent period.

Onomacritus was born in Athens, Greece, but the exact date of his birth remains unknown. He spent most of his life in Athens, where he was deeply embedded in the city's intellectual and political circles. His work on the Homeric epics, particularly the Iliad and the Odyssey, helped establish these foundational texts as cornerstones of Western literature.

The Peisistratid dynasty, to which Onomacritus was closely tied, played a significant role in shaping Athenian politics during the late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE. Onomacritus's collaboration with the Peisistratids underscores the intricate relationships between intellectual pursuits, political power, and cultural expression in ancient Athens.

Onomacritus's legacy extends beyond his work on Homeric texts, as it highlights the complex interplay between textual innovation and political authority in ancient Greece. His story serves as a reminder of the enduring power of intellectual and artistic endeavors to shape our understanding of the past and inform our visions for the future.

Herodotus's account of Onomacritus's exile for interpolating oracles offers a nuanced perspective on the role of prophecy and textual manipulation in ancient Athenian society. This episode underscores the tensions between competing interests and the fluid boundaries between truth, fiction, and historical record.
